drills.q: State the four-phase timebox of the ML/DL depth round.
drills.a: 0-5min warmup calibration, 5-20min classical ML depth, 20-38min deep learning depth, 38-45min open-ended scenario question then close.

drills.q: Train error 2%, test error 25%. Bias or variance, and what's the first move?
drills.a: Variance (the gap is diagnostic, not the absolute train error). First move: more data or regularization, not a bigger model.

drills.q: Two models both have AUC 0.90. Can they behave very differently in production?
drills.a: Yes -- AUC aggregates over every threshold, so two ROC curves can cross and have equal area while one is far better at the specific operating threshold you'll actually deploy at.

drills.q: Derive the L2-regularized linear regression gradient and connect it to a Bayesian prior.
drills.a: Loss = ||y-Xw||^2 + lambda||w||^2, gradient = -2X^T(y-Xw) + 2*lambda*w. Equivalent to MAP estimation with a zero-mean Gaussian prior on w with variance sigma^2/lambda -- larger lambda = tighter, more confident prior toward zero.

drills.q: A boosted model beats a forest on train/test split but underperforms in production 6 months later. First hypothesis?
drills.a: Boosting overfit to the specific residual structure of the training distribution and is more brittle to distribution shift than the forest's variance-averaged, more robust ensemble.

drills.q: MCAR vs MAR vs MNAR -- what changes about your imputation strategy for each?
drills.a: MCAR: mean/median imputation is unbiased. MAR: model-based imputation conditioned on observed variables can be unbiased. MNAR: no imputation is unbiased without modeling the missingness mechanism itself -- the missingness indicator may be the useful feature.

drills.q: Training loss goes NaN at epoch 3. State your diagnostic order.
drills.a: Check exploding gradients (especially RNNs, unclipped), check learning rate too high, check for a hand-rolled softmax/cross-entropy missing the log-sum-exp trick, check for division-by-zero or log(0) from an underflowed probability.

drills.q: How do you evaluate a candidate contextual bandit policy offline before risking live traffic?
drills.a: Off-policy evaluation via inverse propensity scoring: reweight logged rewards by the ratio of the new policy's probability to the old policy's logged probability for the action actually taken. Caveat: high variance when policies diverge a lot -- exactly when you'd want the estimate most.

drills.q: Name three concrete conditions where a simpler model (logistic regression, shallow tree) beats a deep network.
drills.a: Small labeled dataset, a genuine interpretability requirement (regulated lending, medical triage), a latency/serving-cost budget the deep model can't hit, or tabular data where gradient boosting reliably beats deep learning absent very large data.

drills.q: What's the STRONG HIRE bar for the ML/DL depth round, in one sentence?
drills.a: Derives hard mechanisms unprompted (backprop through saturation, softmax+CE gradient, L2-as-prior), names failure modes of their own proposed fixes without being asked, constructs numeric counter-examples proactively.

drills.q: Name the single highest-value derivation in this round, and why it's the one to distrust the rest of the round if missed.
drills.a: The sigmoid vanishing-gradient bound (0.25 max derivative, multiplied across layers via chain rule). If a candidate can't produce this even with the derivative formula given, treat the rest of the deep-learning section skeptically.
